notes: The study's own result matches the claim in substance: Table 2 shows that as drip subsidy rises, aquifer storage gains fall from 74,000 to 40,000 acre-feet/yr and aquifer-to-river gains fall from 32,000 to 17,000, because drip is assumed to produce zero deep percolation (Table 1). However, this is an optimization-model output, not a measured result; the only check against observations is that the base-case technology shares (~90% flood, <10% drip) 'correspond approximately' to actual 2006 EBID conditions, and the recharge/return-flow outputs themselves are never compared with measurements. Crop-level water applied, ET and deep percolation inputs are typical design values. Under the rule that a model run on design data or not checked against observations is 'no', Q2 is answered 'no'; this is a judgement call and the model is otherwise fully basin-scale. Study also notes (footnote **) that where return flows go to saline sinks, reduced applications do save water.
study_notes: The study is a basin-scale hydroeconomic optimization model (Upper Rio Grande / Elephant Butte Irrigation District) run for drip-subsidy scenarios 0-100% over 2006-2025; it reports its own model runs (Q1 yes) but no field measurements. The only comparison with the real system is a statement that the base-case flood/drip shares approximate actual 2006 EBID conditions; the hydrologic outputs (ET, recharge, return flow, depletion) that underlie all claims are not validated against observations and rest on typical crop-level inputs (e.g., drip deep percolation assumed 0). Under the instruction that unvalidated or design-data model runs do not count as own evidence, Q2 is 'no' for all rows; a less strict reader might accept the basin-scale model as evidence for rows 1-3, in which case Q6 (basin/district scale) and Q7 (effect requires return flows to be recoverable, not lost to saline sinks <U+2013> footnote **) would plausibly be 'yes', while Q3, Q4 (ET and return flows are tracked by mass balance), Q5, Q8 and Q9 would largely remain 'no' (no dispersion or uncertainty analysis reported; limitations stated only in footnotes about excluded environmental values). question: q1
evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.9 describe a two-year (2017-2018) split-plot field experiment in a commercial Cabernet Sauvignon vineyard near Benton City, WA, with own measurements. Q2: Section 3.5 and Table 3 report that irrigation method had significant effects on yield in both years, with about 9% (2017) and 12% (2018) higher yield under DRZ than SD across all irrigation rates (SD 9.2/9.3 vs DRZ 10.0/10.4 t/ha). Q4: Section 3.3 and Fig. 3 report midday stem water potential measured by pressure chamber, 10-14% higher under DRZ than SD after veraison in both years; Discussion links lower water stress under DRZ to more resources for aboveground growth and higher yield. Q8: Discussion and Conclusions state the study is an initial step, results are for loamy sand in a semi-arid climate, the proposed mechanisms (reduced evaporation, deep roots) need testing in future studies, and a long-term (e.g. 10-year) study is needed to identify desirable conditions and evaluate benefits.
notes: Yield was measured by one method (hand harvest and weighing) only. One site, one crop, one soil; plot-scale (15-vine plots) only. Soil-texture conditions in the Discussion are drawn from other studies, not the authors' own findings; the root-number interaction with irrigation rate is a variation, not a stated requirement. Table 3 gives yield means with Tukey letters only, no SD/SE/CI; the 9-12% figure is a range across two years, not a dispersion measure. Q4 'yes' rests on stem water potential as the measured intermediate; soil evaporation and soil water in treatment plots were not measured.
study_notes: Full text appears complete. The study compares direct root-zone irrigation (a subsurface drip variant delivering water via vertical PVC tubes at 60 cm) with surface drip irrigation in one commercial vineyard on loamy sand in semi-arid Washington over 2017-2018, with three irrigation rates. Some review passages mislabel the comparator as SDI.

question: q1

question: q2
evidence: Q1: Materials and methods - three-season field trial at Tel Amara station (1997-1999) with drip/fertigation vs macro-sprinkler treatments, randomized block design, 15N microplots, tensiometers, neutron probe and tensionics soil-solution extractors at 30/60/80 cm. Q2: Section 'Nitrate leaching evaluation' and Figure 6 - significantly higher nitrate concentrations below the roots (60 and 80 cm) under sprinkler, while fertigation and drip treatments showed steady very low nitrate at 80 cm and nitrate restricted to the root zone (40 cm); estimated N leached below root zone under 3 kg/ha for drip vs about 55 kg/ha for sprinkler; Abstract and Conclusions repeat that N stayed in the root zone under drip. Q4: 'Fertilizer use efficiency' section - sprinkler described as one-dimensional flow wetting the full bed width; tensiometers showed soil head potential in the upper layer of -175 to -100 mbar under sprinkler and weak fluctuation at 60 cm (-100 to -50 mbar) indicating deeper water penetration; neutron probe showed roots removed relatively more water (39%) from the 30-60 cm layer under sprinkler; irrigation-efficiency calculation estimated 322 mm water lost to subsoil under sprinkler vs 40-50 mm under drip.
notes: Leaching result rests essentially on one method (tensionic soil-solution nitrate at three depths); the leached-N estimate combines the same concentrations with literature-derived irrigation efficiencies, so not counted as independent triangulation. Sprinkler treatment was in a nearby non-randomized area; this is not stated by the authors as a limitation. No dispersion measure is reported for the nitrate concentrations in Figure 6 (only 'significantly higher'); standard errors appear only for shoot dry matter (Figure 3). No condition for the drip effect is stated as a requirement beyond generic recommendations on cost efficiency.
study_notes: Full text appears complete. Study compares drip/fertigation with macro-sprinkler for N recovery and nitrate movement in one Lebanese clay soil over three spring potato seasons.

Q2: Section 3.2 - before drip only 3% of households produced vegetables and 72% of farmers ate no vegetables at meals; after intervention 100% of drip users consumed vegetables with meals; about 30% bought milking cows from vegetable income so milk entered meals; Table 2 - two-thirds of women agreed drip brought changes in daily vegetable intake; Conclusion states drip had a significant positive impact on family food and nutritional intake. Q4: Section 3.3 / Table 5 - vegetable production per household (510 kg), gross income (~US$67) and women's access to and control of cash (92% had no income before) are measured as the pathway to improved food availability (Section 3.2 says improvement is in part because of women's access to income). Q6: Sections 2 and 3.2 - effect reported across a whole village community of 131 adopting households, a 'massive boom' in regional vegetable production. Q7: Section 3.3 - authors state that access to water is the key factor and that market sustenance (IDE-established collection centres) and credit access are also crucial; Conclusion - benefits realised when the technology is offered within a favourable institutional environment; Section 3.4 - expansion difficult where water is scarce. Q8: Conclusion - degree to which outside institutional support made the technology viable is not known; long-term sustainability of the livelihood questionable; returns depend on market prices.

evidence: Q1: Sections 3-4 report the authors' own Tetis hydrological model runs (240 simulations) for the Valencia study area. Q2: Section 3.2.3 states the model was calibrated against observed ETa in flood and drip sectors, monthly groundwater levels in four wells and plot-scale soil moisture (12 behavioural parameterizations); Section 4.3.2 and Figure 8 report control-period mean monthly recharge of 14.3 mm under drip vs 19.1 mm under flood; Section 4.4 reports annual recharge of 169-175 mm (drip) vs 233-248 mm (flood); Conclusion 2 states recharge is higher in flood than drip irrigation. Q4: Sections 3.2.1 and 4.2 describe the modelled soil water storages, irrigation volumes (about 630 vs 490 mm/yr, Figure 4 bars), wetted fraction (53%) and rooting depth that generate recharge, and show recharge peaks in flood irrigation coinciding with irrigation turns. Q6: Section 2 and Figure 1 describe a 913 km2 study area with 68 irrigation sectors (419 km2); results are aggregated at irrigation-sector and regional scale (Figures 8-9). question: q1
evidence: Q1: Chapter 4 'Sensitivity analysis of the ELIDM' (Fig. 45) reports the authors' own model runs of network cost versus number of randomly generated flow regimes for a real Italian network; Annex 1 reports the authors' own calibration of the Clement model using discharges recorded by a Venturi meter at the head of District 4 of the Sinistra Ofanto scheme (Tables A3, A4); Chapter 5 Applications 1-4 report model runs on real networks (582 ha and 1340 ha schemes).
notes: The paper is an FAO design/analysis manual (I&D Paper 59) that also contains original applications, so Q1 is answered yes with some doubt. It does not, however, report any result of its own comparing the investment cost of on-demand networks with that of rotation or other delivery schedules, nor does it attribute a higher cost to guaranteeing peak-period supply. What it shows is related preconditions: the design discharge of an on-demand network must exceed the continuous (24 h) flow by 27-98% depending on r and hydrant elasticity (Fig. 10, Chapter 3), and network cost rises and then stabilises as more flow regimes are included in the ELIDM optimisation (Fig. 45); Chapter 6 states qualitatively that pipe extension to very small holdings is expensive and that O&M charges are somewhat higher than in open-canal systems, without own data. These support a mechanism but not the claimed cost comparison, so Q2 is no and upstream is set true.
study_notes: Full text appears complete (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 59, Lamaddalena & Sagardoy 2000, including Annexes 1-3). The publication is primarily a methodological guideline with an accompanying software package (COPAM); original results are limited to model applications on Italian networks, a sensitivity analysis of optimisation cost versus number of flow regimes, and a field calibration of the Clement formula.

On the claim itself, the study does not compare the investment cost of on-demand networks with that of rotation or other delivery-schedule networks, nor does it report that on-demand networks cost more. It computes network costs for on-demand designs (e.g. 126 million ITL in Box 3, 207 million ITL in Annex 3) and shows (Fig. 45) that optimal network cost rises and stabilises as more flow regimes are required to be satisfied, and it notes (Chapter 3, drawing on FAO Paper 44) that the elasticity eR measures the over-capacity characteristic of on-demand operation; but these are design results for on-demand networks, not an own finding that their investment cost is 'usually higher' than alternatives. Chapter 6 remarks that extending the pipe network to every small farm is expensive, but this is a general statement from FAO (1990), not an own result. Hence Q2 'no'.

question: q1
evidence: Q1: Section 2.2 and Fig. 2 report the authors' own SDrOP model runs for a baseline Kenyan farm case (Table 1); Section 4 reports a seven-day prototype experiment in Cambridge, MA with measured solar, battery, pump and pressure data (Figs. 5-9).
notes: The 18-74% lifetime cost saving and 31-66% reliability gain quoted in the passage come solely from the economic analysis in Section 2.2: a simulation of cost-optimised SPDI designs (SDrOP model, SPM scheduling) for a hypothetical 2 ha tomato farm in Nyeri, Kenya at three well depths, benchmarked against designs from the Grundfos sizing tool operated with SSO. This is a model run on design data; its outputs (life cycle cost, season irrigation reliability) were never compared with measurements from the real system, and the authors state that further validation is needed to show how the economic results change for different conditions. Note also that most of the saving is attributable to the SDrOP design optimisation versus the Grundfos tool rather than to the scheduling approach itself (SPM alone gave +3%, -25%, -18% versus optimised SSO). The seven-day prototype experiment did produce measured results (up to 46% higher solar irrigation reliability on high-demand days, 0.3 kWh vs 1.8 kWh battery buffer, 6-16% pumping energy savings from Level 1), but the comparison was against a simulated SSO reference, no crops were grown, no lifetime cost was measured, and the numbers differ from those in the passage. question: q1
evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.2 and 3 report the authors' own UAV survey (Parrot Anafi, 24 May 2019) over a 0.78 ha maize field at Legnaro, NE Italy, and their own prescription-map outputs (Table 2, Figs 5-7). Q2: Section 3 and Table 2 report that, relative to full-field (blanket) spraying, the area to be sprayed from UAV-derived prescription maps ranged from 14.59% to 2.18% of the field for MLC, 18.92% to 3.75% for ANN and 15.82% to 3.49% for OBIA depending on cell size and threshold. Q7: Discussion states that the effectiveness of the prescription maps is closely tied to matching the detection scale (grid cell) with the spraying equipment available, i.e. sprayers capable of section- or nozzle-level control, and that smaller cells gave lower treated areas only where such precision sprayers exist. Q8: Discussion states that no spraying was carried out, that field trials are still needed to validate the maps under operational conditions, that the study did not compare algorithms technically, that cost-effectiveness studies for Italian farms are missing, and that there is a trade-off between herbicide savings and risk of under-treatment.
notes: The study is on maize, not vegetable crops as the passage states. The passage also misreads the numbers: 2.18%-18.92% is the share of the field that would still be sprayed (i.e. an 81-98% reduction in treated area), not the size of the reduction. The study does not say ANN was more efficient; it says ANN had higher detection sensitivity and produced the largest treated areas (least herbicide saving), while MLC was most conservative. Q3: the three classifiers are applied to the same single RGB orthomosaic with no independent ground check of the area reduction, so one method. Q4: the classification accuracies in Table 1 and the classification outputs are taken from the authors' earlier paper (Mattivi et al. 2021), so no intermediate variable measured in this study. Q5/Q6: single field, crop, season and site. Q9: Table 2 gives point values only, no dispersion.
study_notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a GIS-based desk analysis of prescription maps from one UAV flight; no herbicide application or yield/weed-control outcome was measured, so support is for the computed reduction in area to be treated only.

question: q1

question: q1
evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.5 and 3; the authors run their own SWAP model simulations for a 500 ha district in Northern Italy (2010-2013) using measured canal inflows and bi-weekly piezometer readings, calibrate an empirical percolation-groundwater depth relation (Eq. 7, R2 0.86 calibration, 0.90 validation) and run scenario analyses (Tables 7, 8).
notes: The study does not test drip irrigation at all. It analyses a scenario of switching rice from continuous submergence to flush irrigation (intermittent 150 mm flushes scheduled on demand in SWAP), with maize under border irrigation and poplars. Its finding (Section 3.3.2, Table 7, Conclusions) is that, when the feedback between reduced percolation and groundwater depth is accounted for, flush irrigation lowers summer groundwater by about 35 cm and raises maize irrigation requirements by about 50% (15-day to 10-day turn), so district withdrawal reduction drops from ~80% to ~60%. This matches the effect in the passage but for flush irrigation, not drip; the scenario outputs themselves are model predictions not checked against measurements of the modified system. Technology mismatch therefore Q2 = no and Q3-Q9 = no. evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 and Figures 5-9 - the authors built a 310 g fluorescence LIDAR, mounted it on a DJI Matrice 200 quadcopter and flew it over a ~50 m x 100 m maize plot near Semenovskoe (Moscow region) on 24 June, 17 August and 27 September 2021, reporting their own 680/740 nm chlorophyll fluorescence ratio maps.
notes: The study is a primary instrument-development and feasibility test. It reports only that the drone-borne fluorescence LIDAR can map the 680/740 nm chlorophyll signal over a maize field, that the signal is spatially non-uniform and rises through the season, and that spots of possibly stressed plants can be located. It does not measure yield, productivity, resource-use efficiency, inputs saved or any sustainability outcome; the statements that fast detection 'would allow the prevention of possible crop losses' and that the tool is good for assessing growth and health status are assertions of potential, not results.
